short_definition: A temporary period of supervised work experience offered by employers to students or beginners to provide practical industry exposure.
simple_explanation: An internship is an on-the-job training opportunity that lets you test out a career, learn how a real company works, and build your resume. Internships can be full-time during summers or part-time during school semesters, and in technical fields, they are typically paid.
job_context: Internship postings are designed specifically for current college students or recent graduates with little to no professional experience. Successful internships frequently lead to full-time return job offers.
example: A college junior completes a 10-week summer software engineering internship at a fintech startup, working alongside senior engineers and presenting their project at the end.
source: U.S. Department of Labor (DOL) - Internship Programs Under the Fair Labor Standards Act

short_definition: An ongoing employment arrangement where an employee works a standard schedule (typically 35 to 40 hours per week) and receives full compensation and benefits.
simple_explanation: Full-time employment is what most people consider a standard primary job. In exchange for working roughly 40 hours every week, employees receive a predictable salary, paid time off, and access to company benefits like health insurance and retirement plans.
job_context: Most corporate technology roles are advertised as full-time positions, detailing annual salary, performance bonuses, health coverage, and standard weekly working hours.
example: After graduating from university, an applicant signs an offer for full-time employment as a junior data analyst working 40 hours per week with medical benefits and paid vacation.
source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) - Full-time and Part-time Employment Concepts

short_definition: An employment arrangement where an individual works fewer hours per week than a full-time employee (usually under 30 to 35 hours weekly).
simple_explanation: Part-time jobs offer greater flexibility for people who are balancing school, family, or other commitments. Hours are scheduled across fewer days or shorter shifts, and compensation is often calculated on an hourly basis.
job_context: Part-time tech positions are common for students working in campus IT helpdesks, junior website maintenance roles, or freelance contract engagements.
example: A computer science student works 15 hours a week as a part-time junior web assistant for a non-profit while finishing their university degree.
source: International Labour Organization (ILO) Part-Time Work Convention

short_definition: A designated trial period at the start of employment (commonly 3 to 6 months) during which an employer evaluates a new hire's performance and workplace fit.
simple_explanation: Probation is a mutual evaluation window. It gives the employer time to verify that you can do the job and collaborate well with the team, while giving you time to see if the company and work culture match your expectations.
job_context: Employment offer letters routinely specify a probationary period. Notice periods during probation are often shorter (e.g., two weeks instead of two months), after which employees undergo a confirmation review.
example: A newly hired cloud engineer has a 90-day probation period with monthly check-ins; after meeting all onboarding goals at the 3-month review, their position is formally confirmed.
source: Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development (CIPD) - Managing Probationary Periods

short_definition: The mandatory time duration an employee or employer must provide prior to officially terminating an employment agreement.
simple_explanation: When you decide to leave a company or when a company lets you go, you generally cannot walk out the same day. The notice period (typically 2 weeks to 3 months depending on local labor laws and seniority) gives the company time to find a replacement and hand over tasks smoothly.
job_context: Job application forms frequently ask: 'What is your current notice period?' Recruiters need to know how many weeks or months they will have to wait before a selected candidate can start their new role.
example: A software developer accepts a new job offer and gives two weeks of formal notice to their current manager, using those two weeks to document their code and train their replacement.
source: Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) - Resignation and Notice Practices

short_definition: A formal written invitation from an employer proposing employment to a candidate, detailing position title, compensation, benefits, and start date.
simple_explanation: After you successfully pass your interviews, the company issues a formal job offer letter. It outlines the specific terms of employment—how much you will be paid, your official title, your manager, and your reporting date—for you to sign and accept.
job_context: Candidates should carefully review job offer letters before signing, checking compensation terms, working hours, remote/in-office expectations, and contingencies like background checks.
example: An applicant receives a formal PDF job offer letter for the role of Junior QA Engineer with a stated base salary, 15 paid vacation days, and an official start date on the first Monday of next month.
source: National Association of Colleges and Employers (NACE) Job Offer Guidelines

short_definition: The cumulative practical skills, knowledge, and on-the-job responsibilities gained by an individual across past professional employments.
simple_explanation: Work experience is the real-world track record you build over time. It shows future employers that you have solved actual problems, collaborated with coworkers, met deadlines, and applied academic theories to business projects.
job_context: Job descriptions typically categorize positions by required experience: 0–2 years for entry-level, 3–5 years for mid-level, and 6+ years for senior roles. Internships, capstones, and freelance projects can count toward entry-level experience.
example: A candidate highlights two summer internships and a 6-month university lab research project on their resume to demonstrate one year of relevant hands-on work experience.
source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) - Measures of Work Experience

short_definition: A formal document advertising an open role, outlining core duties, day-to-day responsibilities, mandatory qualifications, and preferred technical skills.
simple_explanation: A job description (often called a JD) is the advertisement companies post when they need to hire. It acts as a shopping list for the ideal candidate, explaining what you would do every day and what skills you should possess before applying.
job_context: Beginners should review job descriptions to identify the core technical skills employers demand, using those requirements to guide their personal learning projects and resume phrasing.
example: An entry-level job description for a Data Analyst lists requirements such as a degree in a quantitative field, proficiency in SQL and Excel, and strong communication skills.
source: Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) - Drafting Effective Job Descriptions

short_definition: A legally binding written agreement between an employee and an employer establishing the rights, duties, compensation, and conditions of the job.
simple_explanation: An employment contract is the legal document both you and the company sign. It covers critical rules including salary, working hours, confidentiality policies, intellectual property rights, non-compete clauses, and grounds for termination.
job_context: Before beginning work on day one, employees sign an employment agreement alongside standard tax forms and non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) to formalize their relationship.
example: A software engineer signs an employment contract that specifies they cannot disclose proprietary company algorithms to third parties and outlines a one-month notice period.
source: International Labour Organization (ILO) Employment Relationship Recommendation

short_definition: A flexible work arrangement where employees perform their professional duties from home or any location outside the employer's physical office.
simple_explanation: Remote work means you do your job from a home desk, co-working space, or library instead of commuting to a corporate office building. You collaborate with your team via video calls, chat apps, and shared online document repositories.
job_context: Many technology job listings explicitly state whether a position is 'Remote', 'On-Site', or 'Hybrid'. Remote listings often emphasize self-motivation, clear written communication, and asynchronous collaboration.
example: A software developer lives in Chicago and works full-time for a technology company based in San Francisco, attending morning team meetings over Zoom and collaborating in Slack.
source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) - Telework and Remote Work Statistics and Definitions

short_definition: A blended working model where employees divide their working days between a physical corporate office and a remote home workspace.
simple_explanation: Hybrid work gives you the best of both worlds. For example, you might go into the office on Tuesdays and Thursdays for face-to-face team brainstorming, and work quietly from home on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays.
job_context: Job postings for hybrid roles usually specify the in-office expectation, such as 'Hybrid (3 days in office, 2 days remote)', requiring candidates to live within commuting distance.
example: A UI/UX designer travels to the downtown office two days a week to run in-person user testing sessions and spends the remaining three days working on wireframes from home.
source: Harvard Business Review & World Economic Forum Future of Work Research

short_definition: Practical training provided by an employer in the workplace to help an employee acquire the specific skills required for their daily duties.
simple_explanation: On-the-job training (OJT) happens while you are working and earning your salary. Rather than studying from a textbook alone, a senior colleague or mentor walks you through internal tools, company workflows, and real projects step by step.
job_context: Entry-level job descriptions often advertise 'comprehensive on-the-job training provided', reassuring candidates that they will be supported as they bridge the gap between academic theory and workplace practice.
example: A newly hired junior systems administrator spends their first month shadowing a senior engineer to learn how to manage the company's internal server monitoring dashboards.
source: U.S. Department of Labor (DOL) Employment and Training Administration
